Article Title: 11-year-old Egyptian girl beats 40 million students in reading contest; what Dubai ruler Sheikh Mohammed did after her win caught attention
Article Text:
Photo courtesy: Gulf News

Photo courtesy: Gulf News

Why did Sheikh Mohammed give Mayar his own badge?

Who is Mayar Othman Al Shourbagy, the girl who beat 40 million students?

A competition that brought together over 40 million students

An emotional victory, a Dh500,000 prize and an unexpected gesture from one of the world's most powerful leaders made 11-year-old Mayar Othman Al Shourbagy's moment in Dubai unforgettable. After she was crowned the winner of the 10th Arab Reading Challenge, Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum removed the badge he was wearing and pinned it onto the young Egyptian student.Mayar had just achieved something remarkable. She emerged as the champion of the 10th edition of the Arab Reading Challenge, beating more than 40 million students from 60 countries. And as she stood before Sheikh Mohammed, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, he did something that went beyond presenting her with a trophy.According to a report by Gulf News, Sheikh Mohammed kissed Mayar on the head, held her close affectionately and then removed his own badge to pin it onto her.While Sheikh Mohammed did not publicly explain the specific reason behind the gesture, it appeared to be a personal expression of appreciation and encouragement for the young champion. The badge was not part of the announced competition prize. Rather, it was a personal gesture from the Dubai ruler as he congratulated the young student on her achievement.When Mayar’s name was announced as the winner, she jumped up in joy, knelt down and kissed the floor in gratitude before breaking down in tears.This was also not the first time Sheikh Mohammed had gifted his badge to a young student. During a visit to Al Ibda'a Model School in Dubai, he had removed his badge and pinned it onto six-year-old Rayyan Badr Mohammed after the boy confidently recited the ruler's full name, as per Gulf News. That badge was a special-edition Expo 2020 Dubai keepsake.Mayar's victory was the result of a reading journey that began at school. The 11-year-old Egyptian student read 60 books during her preparation for the competition and was selected from among 17,616,289 contestants in Egypt. “My journey began at school, when my supervisor noticed that I could speak Arabic confidently and had an enlightened outlook,” Mayar said according to Gulf News.She initially started reading poetry before moving on to books, summarising them with what she described as wisdom, intelligence and precision. “My mother, father and entire family supported me. My school also provided the right environment that enabled me to win this title,” she said. Her achievement earned her the championship title and a cash prize of Dh500,000.The 10th Arab Reading Challenge attracted 40,286,428 students from 60 countries, representing 138,426 schools and 161,507 supervisors. The initiative, launched by Sheikh Mohammed in 2015, aims to encourage reading, strengthen Arabic language skills and nurture a love for knowledge among younger generations.
Article Summary: Mayar Othman Al Shourbagy, 11, won the 10th edition of the Arab Reading Challenge. She beat more than 40 million students from 60 countries. Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum removed his badge and pinned it onto Mayar.

Article Title: Iran to shift uranium stockpile abroad, reopen Hormuz within 7 days under draft deal: Report
Article Text:
Iran-US draft proposes uranium transfer, Hormuz reopening within 7 days

Qatar steps up diplomatic outreach

Trump says US in no hurry to end war

Turkey also engages Washington

NEW DELHI: A preliminary framework for negotiations between the United States and Iran proposes transferring Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country or reducing its enrichment levels, alongside reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding, Al Arabiya English reported on Saturday.The draft framework, which was obtained exclusively by the news platform, also identifies China as a potential guarantor to ensure the implementation and sustainability of any agreement. It proposes holding direct negotiations between Washington and Tehran in Doha instead of Istanbul.Under the proposed arrangement, Iran would undertake commitments on its nuclear programme and maritime security in exchange for US steps to ease sanctions, blockades and other economic restrictions.The framework also envisages an independent verification mechanism to assess compliance before each phase of implementation. This would ensure that neither side makes substantial concessions without corresponding and independently verifiable commitments from the other.A separate dispute-resolution mechanism involving mediators and guarantor countries has also been proposed to address delays or violations and prevent a fresh escalation of military tensions, according to Al Arabiya English.Diplomatic efforts to revive a ceasefire between Washington and Tehran gathered pace on Friday, with a Qatari delegation arriving in the Iranian capital for consultations, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported.The delegation, led by a senior adviser to Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister, arrived on Friday morning and was coordinating its efforts with the United States.Meanwhile, a letter from US Vice President JD Vance to Iranian security official Mohsen Rezaei was reportedly delivered by Qatari envoys. The communication was welcomed in Tehran for proposing a fresh diplomatic pathway to prevent further American military strikes, according to reports.The diplomatic developments come amid US President Donald Trump's assertion that Washington is in no hurry to end its conflict with Iran, describing the hostilities as "not a typical war".Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office, Trump claimed that Tehran remained interested in negotiations but was facing domestic financial difficulties, including an inability to pay military personnel and law enforcement officers.“There are talks. They want to talk. They keep talking,” Trump told reporters.“But look, they're not paying their soldiers, they're not paying their police. They're in a lot of trouble. And we have time, frankly. It's a war, but it's not a typical war; we've been there for seven months,” he added.Trump also played down the financial burden of the military campaign, claiming that Washington's expenditure on the conflict was relatively low and had been offset by gains elsewhere.“We're spending very little money, relatively speaking. I heard somebody say, you're spending money. I said, well, any money we spent, we've more than made up for in a place called Venezuela, like by 10 times...” he said.However, he did not provide figures to substantiate his claim about recovering the cost of the military campaign through Venezuela.Despite expressing confidence that the US had time on its side, Trump has repeatedly raised the possibility of renewed military action against Iran. He previously referred to the prospect of launching “another little Epic Fury”, a reference to the initial US military operation against Tehran, while also suggesting that a “big and good” agreement could still be reached.Parallel diplomatic efforts continued as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of a G20 ministerial gathering in the United States on Friday.According to Turkey's state-run Anadolu Agency, the discussions covered the ongoing negotiations between Washington and Tehran, regional developments and bilateral relations.The meeting followed a telephone conversation between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Trump earlier in the week. During the call, Ankara conveyed its concerns over maritime routes and expressed support for diplomatic initiatives to reduce regional tensions.The proposed framework comes amid continuing differences between Washington and Tehran over Iran's nuclear programme, sanctions and the US blockade of Iranian ports. Whether the latest diplomatic efforts can translate into a lasting agreement remains uncertain.
Article Summary: Draft framework for negotiations between the United States and Iran proposes transferring Tehran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country. It also proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz to international shipping within seven days of an initial understanding. The draft framework also identifies China as a potential guarantor to ensure the implementation and sustainability of any agreement.

Article Title: 'My body hurts, my soul hurts': Christa Pike's first statement after failed execution in US
Article Text:
Christa Pike breaks silence after botched execution

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has said she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on September 30. In her first public statement since the failed execution, the 50-year-old described her injuries, isolation in a prison hospital and uncertainty about her future.In a statement dictated to her lawyers and released on Friday, the 50-year-old said she had been struggling with pain and speech difficulties since the execution attempt.“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak,” Pike said.“And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”Pike, who is being held at the Debra K Johnson Rehabilitation Center in Tennessee, said she had prepared herself to die peacefully but instead regained consciousness alone in a hospital bed.“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next,” she said, adding that she was “searching for meaning in what happened to me”.She also expressed concern for the family of her victim, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer.“I continue to think about my victim’s family,” Pike said, referring to the “terrible pain and loss they have endured”.Pike thanked the first responders and medical staff who treated her, saying support from people around the world had given her strength.“To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words,” she said.Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital during her scheduled execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution on September 30. Her lawyers said the injections may not have entered her bloodstream correctly, instead pooling in her arms and causing severe injuries, including burns and blistering.According to court documents, the execution team struggled to establish functioning intravenous lines. Pike reportedly complained of burning pain before losing consciousness and being transferred to a Nashville hospital in critical condition. She was discharged on October 10.Her lawyers have also asked a federal judge to end her isolation in the prison infirmary, arguing that it violates a 2024 agreement allowing her social contact with other women prisoners. They said the isolation had caused significant psychological harm.Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered officials to preserve evidence relating to the failed execution. Her lawyers have alleged that the incident violated the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.Governor Bill Lee has appointed a former US attorney to review the incident and suspended the state's remaining executions for the year. The move follows another problematic execution attempt in May.Lee rejected Pike's clemency appeal before the execution attempt. Asked about her sentence this week, he said, “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”Pike remains on death row. Her lawyers are seeking to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment.
Article Summary: Christa Pike says she remains in constant physical and psychological pain after surviving a botched lethal injection on September 30. In her first public statement since the failed execution, the 50-year-old described her injuries, isolation in a prison hospital and uncertainty about her future. Her lawyers are seeking to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment.

Article Title: For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton worked as a janitor at a Texas school district and spent her days brightening children’s lives, once believing she had failed because she never went to college; now an el
Article Text:
School did not tell Hampton beforehand it had named the building after her. (Photo: Facebook/Aurbey ISD)

When Hampton learn about the honour

Hampton's extraordinary contributions

What is Marilyn Hampton doing now?

For 39 years, Marilyn Hampton worked as a custodian at a school district in Texas, US, cleaning buildings and helping children whenever she could. She never attended college and once believed she had failed in life because of it. But decades after she began working at the Aubrey Independent School District, the 76-year-old has received an honour she never imagined. According to WFAA-TV, on October 21, officials announced that a new elementary school would be named after her, recognising the years she spent caring for students and supporting the school community.Hampton's journey was not one she had always felt proud of. She grew up in a family of eight children and was the only one among her siblings to complete high school. However, she did not go on to college, something that troubled her for years. She later came to see her life differently, particularly after spending much of it working with children.Her job at the school district involved keeping classrooms and other facilities clean, but Hampton did not limit herself to those responsibilities. She helped children with their assignments, bought school supplies for students who needed them and sometimes gave them rides.She also worked at ticket booths during school football games. These were not part of her regular cleaning duties, but they became part of how she contributed to the district.Hampton retired from her custodial position in 2022 after 39 years of service. By then, she had become a familiar figure to students, teachers and staff members. Her years at the district eventually led officials to make the unusual decision of naming the new elementary school being built in Aubrey after her.The school district did not tell Hampton beforehand that it had decided to name the building after her. Instead, officials invited her to a meeting of the district's board of trustees on October 21. According to The Guardian, she had been asked to attend under the impression that she would be discussing a school-related matter.During the meeting, superintendent Shannon Saylor asked Hampton to unroll a red carpet near the speaker's podium. It was a familiar request for someone who had spent years helping prepare school facilities for different activities.Hampton went ahead with the task. But when she opened the carpet, she found a message she had not expected. Printed across it were the words “Marilyn Hampton Elementary School.”She immediately became emotional as people in the room applauded. Covering her face with her hands, Hampton struggled to respond. “You are too good. I wasn’t expecting this. Thank you all. I can’t speak,” she said, according to the New York Post.Board members came forward to hug her, while officials showed her an image of the new school with her name on the building.Hampton then realised she had not brought her phone to record the moment. Saylor joked that she did not need to worry because the announcement would be shared widely.The district's decision reflected the role Hampton had played in children's lives during her years of service. Although her official job was to maintain school buildings, she often spent time helping students in other ways. Some needed assistance with schoolwork, while others required basic classroom supplies. Hampton helped wherever she could.Her involvement extended to school events as well. She worked at football games and remained connected with the wider school community.Saylor said Hampton had made an important contribution to students despite not holding a teaching position. “She may not have the official title of an educator, but she was in every meaningful sense a teacher and an educator at heart,” the superintendent said.According to The Guardian, thousands of students, teachers and staff members had been influenced by Hampton's commitment during her years at the district.The recognition also meant a great deal to Hampton personally because of her earlier doubts about not attending college.Speaking about how her thinking had changed, she said, “I just thought, ‘You know, Marilyn? God put you where you are supposed to be.’ And I am very happy with the way things turned out.”Although Hampton retired from her custodial job in 2022, she has continued spending time with children. According to the New York Post, she now visits the district's Early Bird Learning Centre, where she has been seen sitting in a rocking chair and feeding a young girl named Claire.Following the school board announcement, the district also presented her with a T-shirt bearing the name of the new elementary school.Hampton later told WFAA that she was still overwhelmed by the recognition. “I still can’t believe it. I haven’t stopped crying,” she said.The new building, previously known as Elementary School Number Five, is scheduled to open in August 2027.
Article Summary: Marilyn Hampton, 76, worked as a custodian at a Texas school district for 39 years. She helped children with their assignments, bought school supplies and gave them rides. She was invited to a meeting of the district's board of trustees on October 21. Officials announced that a new elementary school would be named after her.

Article Title: NOAA awards $8.5 million to restore Hawaii’s Tern Island, where rising seas, storms and wildlife threaten vital seabird nesting grounds
Article Text:
Representative Image of coastal habitat restoration on Tern Island, with seabirds thriving amid conservation efforts and rising sea levels (AI-generated image)

Why Tern Island is important for seabird nesting and wildlife conservation in Hawaii

What NOAA’s $8.5 million Tern Island habitat restoration grant is intended to support

Contaminant cleanup, abandoned buildings and proposed habitat improvements on Tern Island

How rising seas, Hurricane Walaka and wildlife threaten Tern Island seabird habitat

A remote island in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands is set to receive federal funding for coastal habitat restoration as conservation managers confront rising seas, storms and deteriorating infrastructure. On September 10, 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) announced an $8.5 million award to the Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project for work at Tern Island, part of Lalo, also known as French Frigate Shoals. Tern Island has the largest area of available land at the atoll and is identified as a priority landmass for species diversity and population size. Its habitat supports seabirds and other wildlife but is vulnerable to flooding, erosion and damage from animals moving inland. A 2024 report outlines possible restoration measures, including addressing contaminants and derelict structures and improving habitat conditions.Tern Island lies within Lalo, the largest atoll in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands. Tern Island is part of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument and the Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency. Tern Island has the largest amount of available land at Lalo. An earlier state-of-knowledge paper cited in the 2024 Lalo (French Frigate Shoals) Resilience Implementation Options Report identifies it as the priority landmass for species diversity and population size.The island also retains infrastructure from earlier military and US Fish and Wildlife Service occupation, including former barracks, a boat ramp, a runway and a seawall. Some structures have deteriorated, creating potential hazards for wildlife.The island supports black-footed albatrosses, Laysan albatrosses, Bonin petrels and Tristram’s storm petrels. The report notes that a high proportion of the global populations of these four species breed at a small number of sites, many only a few metres above sea level. Tern Island also has a history of long-term wildlife research. The report describes Lalo as having hosted “the most comprehensive and long-term” breeding seabird monitoring programme in the US tropical Pacific. The US Fish and Wildlife Service maintained more than 30 years of data on breeding pairs, breeding seasons and reproductive performance for most of the 21 monument species in its database. Annual monitoring ended after severe weather damaged field research facilities in 2012.NOAA announced the award as part of a wider allocation of $103 million for 16 habitat restoration projects intended to benefit fisheries. The September 10, 2026, announcement names the Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project as the recipient of $8.5 million for coastal habitat restoration at Tern Island. The funding comes from the federal government, not the state of Hawaii. NOAA describes the project broadly as restoring coastal habitat but does not provide a detailed breakdown of the work or confirm that every measure proposed in the 2024 report will be funded through the award.The Papahānaumokuākea Marine Debris Project, a Hawaii-based nonprofit, carries out marine debris removal work across the monument, including efforts to remove discarded fishing gear and other materials that threaten marine wildlife. The 2024 report was prepared for the monument’s management board following a March 2023 workshop involving specialists in climate science, wildlife biology, Native Hawaiian cultural practice and coastal engineering. Its recommendations provide context for the restoration challenges but are not a confirmed list of grant-funded activities.The report identifies contaminant removal as a high-urgency action that should precede longer-term habitat improvements. It discusses options including removing contaminated sediment for disposal in the main Hawaiian Islands, containing remaining contaminants in concrete and considering bioremediation. The work is linked to a separate cleanup effort overseen by the EPA. Its Tern Island Removal Action profile says waste from the former Coast Guard LORAN station was placed in a large dump, while a legacy burn pit contributed high concentrations of polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) to the soil. A Coast Guard cleanup in 2001 was not completed, leaving high PCB concentrations that affected surrounding water and wildlife. The EPA is working with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on the removal action, but its public profile does not establish whether field cleanup has since been completed. Infrastructure modification is another high-urgency priority. The report recommends removing derelict barracks and outbuildings, improving the boat ramp and davit, and establishing a more permanent research shelter. It also proposes breaking up the Tern Island runway to create nesting habitat for burrowing seabirds.The report recommends planning for seawall removal or replacement, subject to further engineering and hydrodynamic studies. Coastal engineering experts at the workshop believed the seawalls could not be removed entirely because currents in the dredged channel on the island’s north side would cause rapid erosion. For habitat stabilisation, the report recommends identifying suitable indigenous plant species to improve nesting and resting areas, provide shade and retain sand. It does not prescribe naupaka for future planting. Instead, it notes that US Fish and Wildlife Service teams have sown naupaka seeds on the island several times since Hurricane Walaka in 2018. The report also recommends coordinating planting with invasive-plant removal and considering a shade house and water catchment system.Hurricane Walaka caused severe damage to East Island, another important nesting site at Lalo, in 2018. Following the loss of vegetation and a black-pipe barrier on Tern Island, Hawaiian green sea turtles moved farther inland to lay their eggs. The report says this movement has increased the destruction of seabird nests and incubating eggs. It also records that monk seals and green sea turtles have wandered inland from beaches into vegetated areas where seabirds nest, contributing to the destruction of nests and eggs. Separately, the report says more frequent use of Tern Island by displaced monk seals has increased disturbance to more sensitive seals, including mothers with pups and moulting individuals, caused by nesting turtles. The report stresses that restoration decisions should account for ecological conditions, engineering constraints and Native Hawaiian cultural perspectives. It also calls for cultural consultation in considering seawall replacement. NOAA’s new award provides funding for coastal habitat restoration, while the specific measures to be implemented at Tern Island remain to be established.
Article Summary: Tern Island is part of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument and the Hawaiian Islands National Wildlife Refuge. A 2024 report outlines possible restoration measures, including addressing contaminants and derelict structures and improving habitat conditions. The funding comes from the federal government, not the state of Hawaii.

Article Title: Watch: NASA’s pencil-thin X-59 supersonic jet spotted flying across US skies
Article Text:
NASA’s experimental X-59 jet

What makes NASA’s X-59 different?

NASA’s pencil-thin X-59 experimental supersonic jet was captured flying over the United States on Wednesday, exactly one year after its maiden flight, as the aircraft began a cross-country journey from California to Florida.Videos of the distinctive aircraft have since surfaced on social media, drawing attention to the milestone. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman responded to one such video on X, writing: “Great catch... X-59 making her way to @NASAKennedy”.The aircraft was en route to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida when it was spotted by people across the US. Videos of the unusual-looking jet were subsequently widely shared on X, drawing attention to its distinctive pencil-thin design. Its journey comes as the space agency marks a year of flight testing for the experimental aircraft, which is the centrepiece of its Quesst mission.The aircraft traveled escorted by an F-15, an F/A-18 and a Gulfstream C-20.NASA Aeronautics also marked the anniversary in a post on X, saying, “One year. New heights. Faster speeds. Since its first flight on Oct. 28, 2025, NASA's X-59 has continued pushing the boundaries of aviation. See how far we've come in just one year!”The agency shared a comparison of the aircraft’s performance on its first flight and one year later.On October 28, 2025, the X-59 reached an altitude of 12,000 feet, clocked a speed of 230 mph and remained airborne for 67 minutes. It had completed just one flight at the time.By October 28, 2026, the aircraft had reached a maximum altitude of 56,000 feet and a top speed of Mach 1.53. Its longest flight lasted 102 minutes, while its flight count had risen to 41, according to the figures shared by NASA Aeronautics.According to NASA, the X-59 is 99.7 feet long and 29.5 feet wide. Its most striking feature is its exceptionally long, narrow nose, which accounts for almost a third of the aircraft’s length. The shape is designed to distribute the shock waves generated during supersonic flight, preventing them from merging into the loud sonic boom commonly heard on the ground.The aircraft is powered by a single engine mounted on top of its fuselage. NASA says this positioning directs engine noise upwards, while the aircraft’s smooth underside helps prevent shock waves from combining.The cockpit is positioned almost halfway along the aircraft and has no conventional forward-facing window. Instead, pilots use NASA’s external vision system, which combines cameras and high-resolution displays to provide a view ahead and below the aircraft.NASA designed the X-59 to fly at Mach 1.4, or approximately 925 mph, at an altitude of 55,000 feet. It is an experimental research aircraft, not a prototype passenger plane, and will never carry passengers.NASA said the X-59’s first flight, piloted by test pilot Nils Larson, took place from the Lockheed Martin Skunk Works assembly site in Palmdale, California, to the agency’s Armstrong Flight Research Center. The initial flight focused on low-speed and low-altitude systems checks.The aircraft is not a prototype for a passenger airliner and will not carry passengers. NASA plans to use it to gather data on the sound generated during supersonic flight and residents’ responses when it flies over selected US communities.NASA said the programme will now move towards acoustic validation, studying the sound produced by the aircraft. The findings are expected to help regulators assess noise standards and the possibility of allowing commercial supersonic flights over land.
Article Summary: The aircraft was en route to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida when it was spotted by people across the US. Videos of the unusual-looking jet were subsequently widely shared on X, drawing attention to its distinctive pencil- thin design. Its journey comes as the space agency marks a year of flight testing for the experimental aircraft.

Article Title: US Marine veteran completes first known thru-hike of proposed Alaska Long Trail, covering 500 miles from Seward to Fairbanks in 47 days
Article Text:
Representative Image of a US Marine veteran hiking Alaska’s rugged Long Trail beneath spectacular mountain views (AI-generated image)

Bradford Bartels’s Alaska Long Trail hike: why the Marine veteran chose the route

How Bartels completed the proposed Alaska Long Trail in 47 days

Why the Alaska Long Trail is still unfinished after its first known thru-hike

US Marine veteran Bradford Bartels, 32, became the first known person to hike the proposed Alaska Long Trail, travelling from Seward to Fairbanks in 47 days and finishing in early August 2026. The route is still being developed and is not yet a continuous, officially established trail. Bartels completed the journey using existing trails, roads and less formal connections, having previously hiked the Appalachian Trail, the Pacific Crest Trail and other long-distance routes. Although he had never spent a night in Alaska’s backcountry, he had considered the challenge for some time. His journey showed that the proposed route could be traversed, even as the wider project remains unfinished. For Bartels, it was also a personal farewell to the life of a thru-hiker.Bartels had been thinking about attempting the route for some time. In an interview with Alaska Public Media, he described Alaska’s backcountry as arguably the greatest on earth and said that, with life being short, it was time to try. He also told Outside: “Thru-hiking needs Alaska, and Alaska needs thru-hiking.” Bartels served as a machine gunner in the US Marine Corps, in military occupational specialty 0331.He joked that people often enjoy firing machine guns more than cleaning or carrying them. His service did not necessarily give him a desire to hike: not every veteran enjoys long marches. But he said it had facilitated his comfort outdoors and helped him become accustomed to discomfort. Carrying a heavy pack through wet and cold conditions was easier to accept when he had chosen the journey himself rather than been ordered to do it.Before setting out, Bartels contacted Mariyam Medovaya, a former Alaska Long Trail program officer, to ask whether the journey was possible. Bartels recalled her answer as “technically doable”. He also sought information from people familiar with different sections of the route. During resupply stops, he asked strangers and local residents, including people wearing camouflage, about trail conditions and where he might have to bushwhack. The Talkeetna Mountains became one of his favourite sections. The route offered glaciers and snow, along with moments he described as frightening. He also recalled the views of Denali from Kesugi Ridge. The journey’s changing terrain gave it a rhythm that he compared to a good song, with a well-timed crescendo.His equipment included a one-person bivy sack, a 70-litre Dyneema roll-top pack, a closed-cell foam sleeping pad, a small isobutane stove and a Dyneema bear bag. He chose synthetic insulation because it performs better when wet. Bartels also paid attention to pack weight, explaining to Alaska Public Media that reducing each pound helped protect his knees. When the load became heavy, he joked that at least he was not carrying a Mark 19, an automatic grenade launcher.Bartels’s journey did not mean the Alaska Long Trail had been completed as an official, continuous route. The Alaska Long Trail project’s FAQ describes a route of more than 500 miles made up of completed trail segments, alternative routes, social routes, water segments and road gaps. It also says a full thru-hike is not possible without significant stretches on roads. The Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Long National Scenic Trail feasibility study describes the proposal as a “multi-braid trail”, combining existing and proposed routes. The agency is assessing whether the route could receive National Scenic Trail designation. Its National Environmental Policy Act project page lists the project as “In Progress - Analysis & Document Preparation”. The BLM has said it is finalising the study for transmission to the Department of the Interior and Congress in the coming months. Establishing a National Scenic Trail requires an act of Congress. Bartels told KTUU that Alaska had seen more ambitious trips, but he did not believe anyone had travelled from Seward to Fairbanks along the proposed route before him. Jane Boer, the Alaska Long Trail program coordinator, told Outside that Bartels “just did it with his feet”. Bartels’s advice to other hikers was straightforward: “You can hike it. And you should.”
Article Summary: US Marine veteran Bradford Bartels, 32, became the first known person to hike the proposed Alaska Long Trail. He travelled from Seward to Fairbanks in 47 days and finishing in early August 2026. The route is still being developed and is not yet a continuous, officially established trail.

Article Title: In 2021, an Ohio couple signed a deal to share house-sale proceeds if they split; after their breakup and a $71,897 dispute, judges upheld the agreement, giving the woman $41,466 despite a fight over
Article Text:
The woman filed an agreement claiming a share of the house-sale money.

House sale turned into court battle

Man refused to share the money

How much money did the woman receive?

A man in Ohio who refused to share money from the sale of his house with his former partner has lost a court battle over an agreement they signed when they were planning to get married. James R Cline argued that his former partner, Ashley A Lokash, had not spent enough money on improving the house to claim a share of the sale proceeds. However, on October 26, an Ohio appeals court ruled in Lokash's favour, allowing her to receive $41,466.50 from the sale.The dispute began with a house the couple bought in Niles, Ohio, in 2021, according to Mortgage Professional America (MPA). At the time, they planned a future together and decided to invest in the property. Although the house was registered only in Cline's name, Lokash agreed to contribute money towards renovations and other improvements. They financed the purchase through a loan guaranteed by the US Department of Veterans Affairs.In September 2021, they signed a written agreement explaining how their money would be handled. Lokash could spend up to $40,000 on improving the property. If the house was later sold, she would first receive reimbursement for her spending, up to the agreed limit.The money remaining after that would be divided equally between them.But their plans changed within months. The relationship ended in March 2022, and Lokash moved out of the house. Cline continued living there and kept furniture that she had purchased. Although they were no longer together, the agreement they had signed remained in place. That became a problem when Cline decided to sell the property.In September 2022, around six months after their separation, Cline put the house up for sale. Lokash wanted to ensure that the money she had contributed would be taken into account when the property was sold.She submitted a copy of their agreement and a written statement to the local property records office so anyone checking the property's records could see that she was claiming a share of the money from its sale. When Premiere Settlement & Title, the company handling the sale, examined the records, it discovered her claim.The house was sold to a buyer in December 2023, but the disagreement continued. The company paid Cline $15,000 and kept another $55,568.51 aside because it could not decide who should receive it.Rather than release the money to either person, the company asked the court to settle the matter. The total amount involved in the dispute was $71,897.61.Cline believed Lokash had not done enough to receive the money promised under their agreement. His argument was that she had agreed to spend money improving the house but had contributed only a small amount compared with the $40,000 mentioned in the document. He therefore argued that the agreement should not be enforced because she had not fulfilled her part of the arrangement.However, the judges found that Cline had misunderstood an important part of what the couple had signed. The agreement did not say Lokash must spend $40,000. It only set that amount as the maximum she could contribute. This meant she could spend less and still meet the conditions of their arrangement.The court examined records showing that Lokash had spent $1,191.34 on materials after the agreement was signed. Her purchases included paint and supplies from Sherwin Williams, items from Handyman and carpeting from Tondo Carpets.Cline also questioned whether these purchases had actually improved the property. But the judges found another problem with his argument. The materials Lokash had bought were in Cline's possession, and he had chosen not to use them. The court concluded that he could not use his own decision not to use the materials as a reason to deny her the money promised under the agreement.After examining the agreement and the couple's spending records, the court upheld the earlier decision in Lokash's favour. The judges found that she had contributed money towards the property and that the agreement did not require her to spend the full $40,000.Lokash was entitled to $11,035.38 as reimbursement for earlier expenses. This included $2,525 she had contributed towards buying the house and $3,325 spent on flooring and carpeting. The remaining amount covered other purchases, including hardware and furnishings.She was also entitled to half of the net proceeds from the house sale, amounting to $30,431.12. Together, these payments brought her total share to $41,466.50.Cline was entitled to the remaining money, including the $15,000 that the company had already paid him.
Article Summary: James R Cline and Ashley A Lokash bought a house together in 2021. Lokash agreed to contribute money towards renovations and other improvements. When the couple split, she filed an agreement claiming a share of the house-sale money. Cline argued that she had not done enough to receive the money promised under their agreement. But an Ohio appeals court ruled in Lokash's favour.

Article Title: Why this US family of nine received a surprise 2026 Chevrolet Suburban after welcoming quintuplets
Article Text:
Image Credit: West Herr New York/Website

How did the arrival of five babies change the Lottbrein family’s daily life

The family faced a practical challenge with transport

West Herr stepped in with a surprise gift

The 2026 Chevrolet Suburban offers room for a growing household

The babies continued to receive care before going home

A family in Buffalo, New York, received an unexpected gift after welcoming quintuplets, turning their household of 4 into a family of 9. The arrival of five babies brought new demands, including the practical challenge of travelling together. West Herr, a car dealership group in the region, stepped in with a new 2026 Chevrolet Suburban to help the parents manage their growing family. The surprise, reported by local news outlets, offered the family some much-needed support during a major change in their lives.Jessica and Jonathan Lottbrein already had two young daughters before their quintuplets arrived. The birth of five more children meant they suddenly had seven children to care for, with their older daughters aged five and one when the babies were born.According to WKBW’s report on the birth, the quintuplets were named Holly, Mason, Stefan, Connor and Layla. They were delivered at Golisano Children’s Hospital of Buffalo on 18 December, arriving between 2.03 am and 2.11 am.The babies were born weighing around two pounds each. Although all five were breathing well at birth, they needed further care before they could leave the hospital. More than a month later, they had grown to around four pounds each, but their medical team continued monitoring their progress.Jessica described the experience as surreal, explaining that watching the babies develop their own personalities while also coming together as a group had been a special experience. The birth also brought a considerable amount of change, as the parents began preparing for life with seven children.One of the biggest questions the Lottbreins faced after welcoming the quintuplets was how they would travel together. A family of nine needs considerably more space than a typical household, particularly when five of its members are babies who require individual car seats.WKBW reported that the parents had two cars between them, but they had effectively been relying on just one while the babies remained in hospital. Their existing GMC Yukon had broken down during a storm while Jonathan was travelling to visit Jessica at the hospital.Jessica recalled that Jonathan had to walk around three miles to reach her after the vehicle stopped working. The incident illustrated how difficult everyday journeys could become when the family was already managing hospital visits and preparing for the babies’ arrival at home.The transport problem was not simply about finding a larger vehicle. The parents needed a practical way to travel with their children while handling the many responsibilities that come with caring for newborns.The solution came from West Herr, a dealership group based in western New York. The company explained that it had learnt about the Lottbreins’ situation and wanted to help.The dealership said Jessica had repeatedly been asked how the family would transport all nine members. Recognising the challenge, the company decided to donate a new 2026 Chevrolet Suburban.According to WKBW, the surprise was arranged after one of the quintuplets had been discharged from Golisano Children’s Hospital. Jessica’s mother contacted Scott Bieler of West Herr, helping bring the family’s transportation difficulties to his attention.Bieler explained that the intention was to remove one major concern from the parents’ minds. The gift was presented as practical support rather than a solution to every difficulty the family might face.Jessica told WKBW that she and her family were shocked and deeply appreciative, as they had never expected to receive such a generous gift. She also explained that the vehicle would make a significant difference when bringing the children home and navigating everyday life.2026 Chevrolet Suburban is a large SUV with three rows of seating. Its size made it a suitable choice for a household that had expanded so quickly.The three-row configuration was intended to help accommodate the children. For the Lottbreins, the extra space offered a more practical way to organise family journeys, including trips involving their 5 newborns and 2 older daughters.The vehicle was particularly relevant because transporting newborns requires more than simply having enough passenger seats. Parents must also accommodate car seats and the equipment needed when travelling with young children.West Herr did not disclose a monetary value for the donated vehicle in its announcement. Instead, the company focused on the family’s immediate needs and its hope that the donation would make daily life easier.The dealership also provided wagons filled with toys and supplies for the quintuplets, along with teddy bears for their older sisters. The additional gifts acknowledged that the change affected the entire family, not just the newborns.While the Suburban addressed the transportation challenge, the quintuplets still needed time to grow stronger before the family could all be together at home.WKBW reported that one baby had been discharged from the hospital when the vehicle was presented, while the other four remained in the neonatal intensive care unit, where medical staff continued caring for them.The earlier birth coverage also highlighted the work involved in safely delivering and caring for five babies at once. Neonatologist Dr Kavya Rao described how a team was ready to assist each infant from birth through stabilisation, with approximately 5 members of staff assigned to each baby.The family was preparing for a major transition, moving from regular hospital visits towards the demands of caring for seven children under one roof. The donated vehicle was intended to make that transition easier when the remaining babies were ready to leave hospital.West Herr’s donation reflected the role that local businesses and relatives can play when a family encounters an unexpected challenge. The company said it was cheering on all five babies as they continued to grow stronger and looked forward to the day when the whole family could be home together.
Article Summary: 2026 Chevrolet Suburban is a large SUV with three rows of seating. Its size made it a suitable choice for a household that had expanded so quickly. The dealership also provided wagons filled with toys and supplies for the quintuplets, along with teddy bears for their older sisters.

Article Title: A Texas woman kept emus, ostriches, goats and 30 chickens on her 14-acre homestead, prompting a feud over property rules; the state's Supreme Court has now blocked her neighbours' broad demand to insp
Article Text:
Representative image

The homestead at the centre

Emu (Representative image)

What the neighbours wanted

The Supreme Court’s decision

Court (Representative image)

Why the case matters

A feud with wider lessons

A long-running dispute over animals, fences and property rules on a 14-acre Texas homestead has ended, at least for now, with a win for the landowner. Pamela Bosco, who kept emus, ostriches, goats and about 30 chickens on her Hays County property, faced a broad legal demand from neighbours seeking access to inspect her land. The Texas Supreme Court has now blocked that demand, ruling that the neighbours did not show a clear legal right to enter and inspect the property. The decision, published in the court’s case record for In re Pamela Bosco, narrows how far neighbours can go when they allege violations of private property restrictions, as per Justia U.S. Law:Bosco’s property was more than a typical residential plot. It was a working homestead of roughly 14 acres, where she raised large flightless birds as well as goats and dozens of chickens. Her neighbours, however, argued that the animals and related activities conflicted with the restrictions governing their subdivision.The disagreement escalated beyond an ordinary neighbourhood complaint. The neighbours sought court-ordered access to Bosco’s land so they could inspect it and gather evidence for their claims. Bosco resisted, arguing that allowing such an inspection would intrude on her property rights without a sufficient legal basis.The dispute eventually reached Texas’s highest civil court.The core issue was discovery, the legal process by which parties obtain information before a trial. The neighbours wanted an order allowing them to enter Bosco’s property to inspect conditions relevant to their allegations. In effect, they sought a broad right of access to land that Bosco owned and occupied.Bosco asked the Texas Supreme Court to stop that inspection order. Her position was that the neighbours had not established that they were entitled to enter her property, particularly when their underlying claims and the scope of the proposed inspection remained disputed. The court agreed that the demand was too expansive to stand as issued.The Texas Supreme Court granted Bosco’s request for relief and blocked the neighbours’ broad inspection demand. The court’s reasoning turned on the principle that a party cannot use discovery to obtain access to private property without first showing a proper legal basis for that access.In practical terms, the ruling does not necessarily decide whether Bosco’s animals or homestead activities violate the subdivision’s restrictions. Instead, it decides that the neighbours cannot compel a wide-ranging physical inspection of her land simply by asserting that such an inspection might support their case. They must pursue their claims through the ordinary legal process and meet the required standards before seeking intrusive access.The decision is significant for rural and semi-rural landowners across Texas, where homesteads often sit near newer residential developments and where neighbours may disagree about noise, animals, fencing, drainage or the character of a neighbourhood. Property restrictions can be enforceable, but the Texas Supreme Court’s ruling makes clear that enforcing them does not automatically give neighbouring owners a licence to enter someone else’s land.It also highlights the difference between alleging a violation and proving one. A neighbour may believe that emus, ostriches, goats or chickens breach a deed restriction, but the courts require evidence gathered through lawful means. The ruling signals that inspection of private property is an exceptional remedy, not a routine tool for gathering leverage in a neighbourhood dispute.For Bosco, the ruling preserves her ability to continue using her homestead while the underlying dispute is resolved through proper legal channels. For her neighbours, it means their case cannot rely on a sweeping inspection order unless they satisfy the court that such access is justified. The Texas Supreme Court’s decision therefore draws a boundary between legitimate enforcement of property restrictions and an overbroad intrusion into private land.The case is also a reminder that rural living can involve legal friction as communities change. A 14-acre property with exotic birds, goats and poultry may be entirely ordinary to one owner and incompatible with another’s expectations. But Texas’s highest court has made clear that resolving those tensions must begin with respect for property rights and adherence to legal procedure, not with unrestricted access to a neighbour’s land.
Article Summary: Pamela Bosco kept emus, ostriches, goats and about 30 chickens on her 14-acre Texas homestead. Neighbours argued that the animals conflicted with the restrictions governing their subdivision. The neighbours sought court-ordered access to Bosco’s land so they could inspect it and gather evidence for their claims. Bosco resisted, arguing that allowing such an inspection would intrude on her property rights.

Article Title: 'Not an anti-China coalition’: US clarifies Quad’s position amid regional tensions
Article Text:
Rubio described the Quad as a cooperative arrangement between four countries that share common interests

Quad foreign ministers pledge closer cooperation

US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said the Quad is not an alliance directed against any country, while noting that the grouping's concerns over certain actions and behaviours repeatedly point to one nation. Though he did not name the country, his remarks come amid growing concerns over China's activities in the Indo-Pacific.“The Quad is not anti-anybody. It’s not a format that exists to be against any country,” Rubio told reporters in Atlanta. He said the grouping's concerns were directed at specific behaviours and activities rather than any particular country.“Now, those activities or behaviours are coming repeatedly from one country. That’s going to be obvious to everybody,” he said, while reiterating that the Quad was not an “anti-China or anti-anybody coalition”.Rubio described the Quad as a cooperative arrangement between four countries that share common interests and oppose certain actions. He did not identify the country he was referring to. The joint statement issued after the meeting also refrained from naming any nation.He further said a meeting of Quad leaders would take place in Manila in November, adding that an announcement on the dates was expected soon.He did not provide further details.Foreign ministers from India, the US, Australia and Japan met in Atlanta, Georgia, on Saturday, reaffirming their commitment to cooperation across supply chains, maritime security and emerging technologies.In their joint statement, the four countries announced more than $85 million in technical and financial assistance to expand access to what they described as trusted artificial intelligence across the Indo-Pacific. The initiative will include a Quad AI Accelerator.The ministers also expressed “grave concerns” over economic coercion, including arbitrary export restrictions and excess production capacity driven by non-market practices. They underlined the importance of resilient supply chains and cooperation in critical technologies.On maritime security, the statement stressed that navigation rights in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait must be protected under international law. The ministers also opposed the imposition of tolls on international shipping, citing provisions of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Article Summary: Rubio described the Quad as a cooperative arrangement between four countries that share common interests and oppose certain actions. Foreign ministers from India, the US, Australia and Japan met in Atlanta, Georgia, on Saturday, reaffirming their commitment to cooperation across supply chains, maritime security and emerging technologies.

Article Title: Meet Atiksh Bhan, the student who tested different incentives to reduce smartphone use during face-to-face conversations in a randomised trial
Article Text:
Atiksh Bhan. Image Credit: Regeneron ISEF

What did Atiksh Bhan investigate through his smartphone use study

How did the student conduct the research

Phubbing is an important social concern

What did the trial reveal about changing phone habits

Atiksh Bhan was recognised at the 2026 science fair

Smartphones are ubiquitous today in social interactions, frequently competing for attention even when people are sitting together. Student researcher Atiksh Bhan explored whether simple incentives could motivate people to put away their phones when talking face-to-face. His project, titled Designing for Presence, explored different ways of reducing smartphone use through a randomised trial. The research focused on how small changes in behaviour and the way people are encouraged can help make in-person interactions more attentive and meaningful.Atiksh Bhan, a student from Manassas, Virginia, chose to examine a behaviour that has become familiar in homes, schools, restaurants and public spaces. Known as phubbing, it describes the habit of looking at or using a smartphone while interacting with someone in person. Rather than simply asking people to switch off their devices, Bhan investigated whether incentives could encourage them to give more attention to the people around them. His research brought together social behaviour, mental health and practical ways to encourage change.The project, titled ‘Designing for Presence: A Randomised Controlled Trial Comparing Incentive Structures to Reduce Smartphone Use During Social Interactions,’ examined how different forms of encouragement could influence phone use during conversations.According to the Society for Science, phubbing affects an estimated 75% of smartphone users. The behaviour has also been associated with depression, loneliness and dissatisfaction in relationships. These connections made the subject relevant beyond everyday phone etiquette, giving Bhan an opportunity to explore how technology habits can affect people's social experiences.Bhan used a randomised controlled trial to study smartphone behaviour in real social settings. According to the Society for Science, the study involved 132 adults, of whom 62% were women.Instead of restricting the research to an artificial laboratory setting, he observed existing social groups in public spaces. The observation sessions lasted an average of 75 minutes, allowing him to examine phone-related behaviour during ordinary social interactions.The reason we randomised was because the project was about comparing different incentive structures, not about people’s opinions on their smartphone habits.Bhan might also study behaviour in groups, looking at how the presence and actions of other people could affect an individual’s willingness to put a phone away.Smartphones make it easy to communicate, access information and stay connected. However, their constant availability can also interrupt conversations that take place in person.Phubbing describes precisely this situation. Even a brief interruption can change the experience of a conversation, particularly when one person feels that their attention is being divided.Instead of treating smartphone use as a habit that people must simply abandon, the project considered whether the surrounding social environment could help encourage different choices.This is an important distinction, because using your smartphone isn't always a conscious choice to ignore someone. They merely check their notifications because they are used to it or feel they should be available. Understanding these patterns can help researchers explore more practical ways to encourage attentive interactions.One of the important observations from Bhan's research was that incentives alone might not explain why people change their behaviour. The Society for Science reported that the findings pointed towards the influence of interdependent group dynamics.In simple terms, the decisions people make about using their phones might be affected by what other people in their social group are doing. When people are in groups their behaviour can affect each other. This suggests that encouraging a whole group to remain engaged could be more effective than focusing exclusively on individual phone users.The research demonstrated a new approach known as contingency management, which uses incentives to encourage a desired behaviour. According to the Society for Science, the approach could be applied in cafeterias, at events and in other social environments where people gather.Bhan's work received recognition at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), where he competed in the behavioural and social sciences category.According to the Society for Science, his project received the second award, worth $2,400. He represented Charles J. Colgan Sr. High School in Virginia and qualified through the Prince William-Manassas Regional Science and Engineering Fair.The competition brought together high school students who had earned their places by winning awards at affiliated local, regional, state or national science fairs. The 2026 edition was the 76th annual event.Bhan's project also appeared in the organisation's special awards announcement. The May 15 report listed him among the recipients of complimentary student affiliate memberships under the American Psychological Association's recognition programme.The research does not suggest that smartphones are inherently harmful or that every instance of checking a device damages a relationship. Smartphones are unlikely to disappear from everyday interactions, but the way people use them around others can influence the quality of those experiences.
Article Summary: Student researcher Atiksh Bhan explored whether simple incentives could motivate people to put away their phones when talking face-to-face. His project, titled Designing for Presence, explored different ways of reducing smartphone use through a randomised trial. Bhan's work received recognition at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF)

Article Title: 1 killed, several injured in shooting at US stadium after Alabama football game
Article Text:
Gunfire at US stadium after Alabama football game leaves 1 dead

One person was killed and several others were injured in a shooting in Alabama's Birmingham on Saturday night, shortly after the Magic City Classic football game ended.Gunfire broke out around 7:50 pm (local time) at Legion Field stadium, AL.com reported.The Jefferson County Coroner’s Office confirmed to the local publication that at least one person had died. Authorities have not yet disclosed the total number of people injured.According to public safety radio communications, at least two people were critically injured, while another person suffered minor injuries.The shooting took place shortly after the Magic City Classic, the largest historically Black college and university (HBCU) football game in the US, concluded at the stadium. The annual match is played between Alabama A&M University and Alabama State University.Following the shooting, authorities suspended all tailgating activities and directed people to leave the area around the stadium.
